596.title: Like a dream and a show
596.word: Like a dream and a show
596.hook: know this world like a dream and a show; none of it is true without the Lord (Salok M9, ang 1427)
596.howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok at the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib; teachers often read it beside Guru Arjan's line that the Lord is true and all He made is true, so that the world is honored and held lightly at once.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-NINETY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, fear none, and your line: frighten none, fear none. Did you lower your voice in a tense moment and still stand firm? What makes that kind of courage possible? Part of the answer is in today's salok. Day five hundred ninety-six.
screen: `FEAR NONE — FRIGHTEN NONE, FEAR NONE.`

segments.voice: You're in a dream, and it's urgent. You've missed the exam, or the train is leaving, or you're back at an old school and can't find the classroom. Your heart is pounding. It is completely real. Then your eyes open. The ceiling. The alarm clock. Your own bed. And in about three seconds, the whole drama drains away, and you almost laugh. It was so real a moment ago. Now it's nothing you need to fix. Guru Tegh Bahadur's salok asks what it would be like to see the whole world with those first waking eyes.
screen: `THE DREAM: URGENT AND REAL.` → `EYES OPEN: THE CEILING.` → `WAKING EYES.`

segments.voice: The salok says jio supnaa ar pekhnaa, aise jag kau jaan. In paraphrase: like a dream and a show, know the world to be so. In all of it, nothing is saacho, true, says Nanak, except the Lord. Supnaa is a dream. Pekhnaa is a show, a spectacle, the kind of street play or puppet performance a crowd gathers to watch. It's vivid, it pulls you in, you might even cry. And then the curtain drops and everyone goes home. Two pictures of the same thing: an experience that feels total while it lasts, and then ends. Now, this salok needs to be heard alongside the rest of the Granth. In Sukhmani, Guru Arjan says that the Lord is true, and everything He has made is true. So Sikh teaching doesn't call the world a lie in the sense of fake. Both lines are in the same scripture, and Sikh teachers hold them together. The world is real as the Lord's creation, and passing as a dream is passing. Read beside Sukhmani, saacho here points to what lasts. What isn't true is our grip on the world, the way we take the show for the whole of reality. Now go back to yesterday's courage. Sikhs remember Guru Tegh Bahadur facing the empire's threats in Delhi without fear, and some readers hear this salok as part of the reason: he saw those threats with waking eyes. Real, yes, and terrible. But not the thing that lasts. The dream isn't worthless. It just isn't the place to build your whole life. Wake up inside it, and you can play your part in the show without forgetting it's a show.
screen: `SUPNAA: A DREAM.` · `PEKHNAA: A SHOW ON A STREET.` · `TRUE AS HIS, PASSING AS A DREAM.` · `WAKING EYES, EVEN IN DANGER.` · then, large: `LIKE A DREAM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember a dream from last night. Close your eyes and try to recall any dream, even a fragment: a place, a face, a feeling. If nothing comes, recall any vivid dream you've ever had. Notice how real it felt, and how quickly it faded on waking. Then open your eyes and look around the room with the same fresh, waking eyes. The chair, the light, your hands. Real, and passing. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths, the One the salok says remains. The bell holds the time.
Like a dream and a show. The salok asks us to know the world like supnaa, a dream, and pekhnaa, a show: vivid, real while it lasts, and passing, while the Lord remains.
screen: `LIKE A DREAM AND A SHOW — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: like a dream. Today, when something feels like the end of the world, take a waking breath, and ask how it will look a year from now. Day five hundred ninety-six.

screen: `DAY 596 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YOUTH HAS GONE.`

597.title: Youth has gone
597.hook: youth passes and old age conquers the body (Salok M9, ang 1428)
597.howItsDone: Sikhs hear the ninth Guru's saloks on youth and old age at the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib; in the gurdwara, children, adults and elders sit and sing together.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-NINETY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, like a dream and a show, and your line: like a dream. Did you take a waking breath when something felt huge? Of all the shows we watch, the one we watch most closely is in the mirror. Today, the body's years. Day five hundred ninety-seven.
screen: `LIKE A DREAM AND A SHOW — LIKE A DREAM.`

segments.voice: A shop window catches your reflection, unexpectedly, and for half a second the person in it is a stranger. Then the face comes into focus. When did that happen? The gray at the temples, the line between the eyebrows, the oof that now comes with sitting down. The calendar keeps one count; the mirror keeps another. A whole industry promises to stop the clock. Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks don't sell anything. They just tell the truth about the clock, and then ask a better question.
screen: `A STRANGER IN THE SHOP WINDOW.` → `THE MIRROR KEEPS ITS OWN COUNT.` → `THE CLOCK, TOLD TRUTHFULLY.`

segments.voice: One of the early saloks begins tarnaapo io hee gaio, leeo jaraa tan jeet. In paraphrase: youth has passed away just like that, and old age has conquered the body. Tarnaapo is youth, the years of strength. Io hee, just like that, without anyone noticing. And jaraa is old age, pictured as a conqueror that has taken the body's territory. It's an honest line. No softening. But listen to the salok's second line, which we met on day five hundred ninety: says Nanak, O mind, turn to the Lord, the time is slipping by. Old age in these couplets isn't the enemy to be defeated. It's a teacher pointing at the clock. The question isn't how to stay young. It's what you're doing with the age you are. That's where today's line comes from: every age is His. Sikh life has room for every stage. Children learn to sit in the sangat and sing. Young people work, marry, raise families, and serve. Elders are honored for what they've carried. Each age can remember the Lord in its own way. A child's simple Waheguru. A parent's tired prayer at the end of a long day. An elder's slow, steady simran. None is second best. The salok tells us youth goes. It doesn't tell us anything is lost that can't be offered at the next age. So the body changes its count. The soul's work, remembering, is the same at seven, at thirty-seven, at seventy-seven. Every age is His.
screen: `TARNAAPO: YOUTH, GONE JUST LIKE THAT.` · `JARAA: OLD AGE, THE CONQUEROR.` · `NOT HOW TO STAY YOUNG.` · `EACH AGE REMEMBERS IN ITS WAY.` · then, large: `EVERY AGE IS HIS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank your body at its age. Sit comfortably and scan slowly from feet to head. Wherever you notice something that's changed with the years, a stiff knee, tired eyes, a sore back, pause there. Instead of resenting it, thank it. Thank the feet for every mile. Thank the hands for everything they've carried. Thank the heart for beating through every year so far. If you pray, you can thank Waheguru for this body, at exactly this age. The bell holds the time.
Youth has gone. The salok says youth passes just like that, and jaraa, old age, conquers the body; and every age can still turn to the Lord.
screen: `YOUTH HAS GONE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: every age is his. Today, when you notice your age, a creak, a gray hair, a birthday, say the line and offer the age you are. Day five hundred ninety-seven.

screen: `DAY 597 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HEAD SHAKES, FEET STAGGER.`

598.title: Head shakes, feet stagger
598.hook: the head shakes, the feet stagger, the eyes grow dim; still you don't turn (Salok M9, ang 1428)
598.howItsDone: Sikh families honor elders, who often lead the household's prayers and teach children the Gurbani they know by heart; this salok is heard at the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-NINETY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, youth has gone, and your line: every age is his. Did you thank your body at its age? Yesterday said every age can turn to the Lord. Today's salok asks why, so often, we don't. Day five hundred ninety-eight.
screen: `YOUTH HAS GONE — EVERY AGE IS HIS.`

segments.voice: Here's a someday list. Someday I'll call my brother and make peace. Someday I'll learn to read Gurmukhi properly. Someday I'll sit quietly every morning. Someday, when the kids are older, when work calms down, when I retire. The list is kind to us. It never says no. It just says later. And later has a way of turning into a doctor's waiting room, a walker by the door, glasses that don't quite help. Guru Tegh Bahadur's salok paints that later with a few quick strokes, and then asks a question that stings.
screen: `THE SOMEDAY LIST.` → `IT NEVER SAYS NO, ONLY LATER.` → `LATER, PAINTED IN A FEW STROKES.`

segments.voice: The salok says sir kampio pag dagmage, nain jot te heen. In paraphrase: the head shakes, the feet stagger, the eyes have lost their light. Says Nanak, this is what has happened, and still the mind isn't absorbed in the Lord's love. Sir is the head. Kampio, it trembles. Pag dagmage, the feet totter. Nain jot te heen, the eyes without their light. It's a portrait of great age, drawn in three short strokes. But read the line carefully, because it's easy to hear it wrong. The salok is not mocking old people. The body's weakness isn't the problem in the line at all. The problem is the last half: tau na har ras leen, still not absorbed in the Lord's sweetness. The body has been sending signals for years, and the mind has been saying later. So the salok isn't about the elderly. It's about the someday list, held by people of every age. And it's one reason Sikh families honor their elders. Some of them did turn while they could. They're the ones who taught grandchildren the Mool Mantar, who kept the morning prayers when no one else was awake, whose shaking hands still fold for Ardas. A Sikh elder at the gurdwara, head trembling, singing every word of a shabad from memory, is the opposite of this salok's warning. Their body staggered. Their mind didn't wait. So the line is less a threat than an invitation. The body's clock is running whatever we do. The mind can still choose. Turn while you can.
screen: `SIR KAMPIO: THE HEAD SHAKES.` · `PAG DAGMAGE: THE FEET TOTTER.` · `THE MIND STILL SAYS LATER.` · `ELDERS WHO DIDN'T WAIT.` · then, large: `TURN WHILE YOU CAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor an elder. Bring to mind an older person in your life, a grandparent, a neighbor, a teacher, someone in the sangat, living or gone. Picture their hands, their voice, something they taught you without meaning to. Silently thank them. Then pick one way to honor them this week: a call, a visit, asking them to tell you a story, or, if they've passed, doing one thing the way they did it. If you pray, you can hold them before Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Head shakes. The salok draws great age in three strokes, head, feet, eyes, and warns not about the body but about a mind that keeps saying later.
screen: `HEAD SHAKES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: turn while you can. Today, take one item off your someday list and do the first small step now. Then call an elder, if you can. Day five hundred ninety-eight.

screen: `DAY 598 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE NAME CARRIES ACROSS.`

599.title: The Name carries across
599.hook: the Name is the boat across the world's ocean (Salok M9, ang 1428)
599.howItsDone: Many Sikhs repeat Waheguru, quietly or aloud, in moments of fear or worry, and speak of the Name as the boat across the world's ocean, an image found throughout the Guru Granth Sahib.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-NINETY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, head shakes, and your line: turn while you can. Did you take one step off your someday list? Turn toward what, though, and how does it help? Today's image is a boat. Day five hundred ninety-nine.
screen: `HEAD SHAKES — TURN WHILE YOU CAN.`

segments.voice: It's three in the morning, and the worry has arrived. Money, a test result, a child far away, the thing you said that you can't unsay. The room is dark and the thoughts are loud. Each one pulls you further out, like a swimmer caught in a current, and the shore keeps getting smaller. Thinking harder doesn't get anyone out. In this picture, thinking is the water. What you need is something that floats. Gurbani has an old answer for this, and Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks reach for it again and again.
screen: `3AM: THE WORRY ARRIVES.` → `A SWIMMER IN A CURRENT.` → `SOMETHING THAT FLOATS.`

segments.voice: Across the Guru Granth Sahib, the world is pictured as an ocean: bhav saagar, the ocean of existence, sometimes bhau nidh, the terrifying sea. It's deep, it's wide, and it's full of waves: desire, fear, grief, the endless round of coming and going. In Gurbani's picture, nobody swims it on their own strength. And the way across is the Name, Naam, the remembrance of the Lord, pictured as a boat. In the ninth Guru's saloks, the call keeps coming: says Nanak, O mind, meditate on the Lord, and you'll cross the terrifying ocean. We heard it at the end of the salok about the Lord in every heart. Notice what a boat is. It doesn't empty the ocean. The waves stay. The storm can still come. But you're carried on top of it instead of pulled under. Sikhs use this picture for simran. The worries at three in the morning don't vanish when someone repeats Waheguru; what Sikhs describe is having something under them now. Think back to Makhan Shah, at the start of this block. Tradition says that when his ship was caught in a storm, he turned to the Guru, and the ship came through. Sikhs tell that story as history and as a picture at the same time. Every ship meets a storm sooner or later, and in Sikh teaching the Name is what keeps a person afloat while it passes. And a boat has one more lesson. You have to get in. Admiring it from the shore doesn't carry anyone across. In the saloks, the one who crosses is the one who remembers, who actually says the Name, especially in the worried hour.
screen: `BHAV SAAGAR: THE WORLD'S OCEAN.` · `NAAM: THE BOAT ACROSS.` · `THE WAVES STAY; YOU FLOAT.` · `YOU HAVE TO GET IN.` · then, large: `THE NAME IS THE BOAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember the Name once in worry. Sit and let one current worry come up, the one that keeps pulling at you. Feel where it sits in the body. Don't try to solve it. Instead, on the next breath, if you pray, say Waheguru, slowly, once on the in-breath and once on the out-breath. If you don't pray, rest on one steady word, like here. Let the worry stay. Notice that something is holding you up while it does. The bell holds the time.
The Name carries across. In the ninth Guru's saloks, the world is a terrifying ocean, and remembering the Lord's Name is the boat that carries you over the waves.
screen: `THE NAME CARRIES ACROSS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the name is the boat. Today, the next time worry pulls you out, don't swim harder. Say the Name once, or one steady word, and let it carry you. Day five hundred ninety-nine.

screen: `DAY 599 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE WORLD'S CREATION IS FALSE.`

600.title: The world's creation is false
600.hook: jag rachnaa sabh jhooth hai: know, friend, that this created world is passing (Salok M9, ang 1429)
600.howItsDone: This salok is among the ninth Guru's saloks read at the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib; Sikh teachers explain its jhooth as 'not lasting' rather than 'fake', pointing to its image of a wall of sand.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Name carries across, and your line: the name is the boat. Did you say the Name, or one steady word, when worry pulled? Today is day six hundred, and the salok we reach uses a word that's easy to misunderstand. Day six hundred.
screen: `THE NAME CARRIES ACROSS — THE NAME IS THE BOAT.`

segments.voice: When a friend tells you a promise is false, you know what they mean: it was a lie. Someone set out to fool you. So if you open an English translation of today's salok and read that the world's creation is false, it sounds startling. Is the scripture saying the sunrise is a lie? Your grandmother's hands? The bread on the table? That's not how Sikhs hear it. The key is in the second half of the couplet, and in a picture anyone who has played with dry sand knows: pile it into a wall, and it starts slipping the moment you take your hands away.
screen: `FALSE: A LIE?` → `THE SUNRISE, THE BREAD, THE HANDS.` → `THE SECOND HALF OF THE COUPLET.`

segments.voice: The salok says jag rachnaa sabh jhooth hai, jaan lehu re meet. In paraphrase: all the world's creation is jhooth; understand this, O friend. Then: says Nanak, it does not stay steady, like a wall of sand. Jhooth is usually translated false. But look at how the salok explains itself. It doesn't say the world is a trick. It says thir naa rahai: it doesn't stay put. And it gives the picture: baaloo kee bheet, a wall of sand. A sand wall isn't a lie. It's really there. You can touch it, lean on it for a moment. It just won't hold. That's the sense of jhooth here: not fake, but not lasting. Something you can't build your whole weight on. Remember rachnaa, too. On day five hundred eighty-one we heard rachnaa raam banaaee, the creation the Lord made. Same word. The creation is His. What's jhooth is the idea that it will stand forever. And listen to the tone: re meet, O friend. The Guru isn't lecturing a sinner. He's talking to a friend, the way you'd gently tell someone you love not to lean a ladder against loose sand. So today's line, hold it lightly, isn't a call to despise anything. Enjoy the house. Love the people. Do the work well. Just don't lean your whole life against a wall that's already slipping at the top. Lean on what stays, the Name we heard about yesterday. Six hundred days in, that's worth hearing: everything here is lent, and the lender is the One who stays.
screen: `JAG RACHNAA SABH JHOOTH HAI.` · `THIR NAA RAHAI: IT DOESN'T STAY.` · `BAALOO KEE BHEET: A WALL OF SAND.` · `RE MEET: SAID TO A FRIEND.` · then, large: `HOLD IT LIGHTLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let go of one attachment. Sit and breathe slowly. Think of one thing you've been leaning on with your whole weight: a plan, a status, an outcome you've decided must happen, someone's approval. Picture it as a wall of sand you're pressed against. Now, gently, take one step back. You don't have to knock it down. Just stand on your own feet, near it, not against it. Feel the ground under you. If you pray, you can lean on Waheguru instead, for these breaths. The bell holds the time.
The world's creation is false. The salok calls the world jhooth, not because it's fake, but because, like a wall of sand, it doesn't stay steady, and it says so as one friend to another.
screen: `THE WORLD'S CREATION IS FALSE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: hold it lightly. Today, with one thing you care about, enjoy it fully and lean on it a little less. Day six hundred.

screen: `DAY 600 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: RAMA GONE, RAVANA GONE.`

601.title: Rama gone, Ravana gone
601.hook: raam gaio raavan gaio: Rama went, and Ravana with his large family went too (Salok M9 50, ang 1429)
601.howItsDone: This salok is read near the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib; Sikh teachers explain it as a reminder that even the greatest figures of the old stories departed, so no one's status lasts.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the world's creation is false, and your line: hold it lightly. Did you lean a little less on one thing you care about? Yesterday's salok said nothing stays, like a wall of sand. Today's names names. Day six hundred one.
screen: `THE WORLD'S CREATION IS FALSE — HOLD IT LIGHTLY.`

segments.voice: Every autumn across north India, at Dussehra, crowds gather in open fields to watch giant effigies of Ravana, the ten-headed king of Lanka in the Ramayana, go up in flames. Children sit on their parents' shoulders. Fireworks crack inside the figure. And the story behind it, of Rama, the hero king, and his long war with Ravana to win back Sita, is one of the best-known stories in South Asia. Everyone in Guru Tegh Bahadur's world knew it. So when one of his saloks opens with those two names side by side, his listeners would have sat up. What could he possibly be saying about them?
screen: `DUSSEHRA: RAVANA IN FLAMES.` → `RAMA, THE HERO KING.` → `TWO NAMES SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: The fiftieth salok says raam gaio raavan gaio, jaa kau bahu parvaar. In paraphrase: Rama went, and Ravana went, who had such a large family. Says Nanak, nothing stays steady; the world is like a dream. Gaio means went, departed. Parvaar is family, the whole household. Ravana, in the epic, had a vast family and kingdom. And the salok's point is very simple: the greatest hero in the story, and the greatest villain, both left this world. The good king and the proud one, the one people worship and the one they burn. Death took both. Here it's worth saying who believes what. For many Hindus, Rama is God come to earth, deeply loved and worshipped. Sikh teaching speaks of God as never born and never dying, and Sikhs read this salok as being about Rama the king in the story, a man who walked the earth and left it. The salok isn't mocking anyone's faith. It's using the most famous names anyone knew to make the plainest point there is. And that's how it lands. If even they went, the hero with all his virtue, the villain with all his power and his huge family, then nobody's status, goodness or strength buys a longer stay. It's not meant to make us gloomy. It's meant to make us honest. Our own name, our own family, our own little kingdom, will go the same way. What lasts, as we've heard again and again in these saloks, is the Name of the Lord. Even they went. So, gently, will we.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of the great who passed. Sit quietly and bring to mind three people who once seemed larger than life: a famous leader, a great artist, someone in your own family everyone looked up to. Picture each one at the height of their strength. Then remember that each has gone, or will. Let it be calm, not sad. Then turn to your own life with the same honesty: this, too, will pass. What would you like to fill it with? If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths. The bell holds the time.
Rama gone. The fiftieth salok says Rama went, and Ravana with his great family went too; nothing stays steady, and the world is like a dream.
screen: `RAMA GONE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: even they went. Today, when you feel very important, or very small, remember the line, and spend the next hour on what lasts. Day six hundred one.

602.title: Worry about the unexpected
602.hook: worry only about what cannot happen; this is the world's way, nothing stays (Salok M9 51, ang 1429)
602.howItsDone: Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks are read near the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikh teachers cite salok fifty-one as a word against needless worry.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama gone, Ravana gone, and your line: even they went. Did someone great come to mind? This week ran like a dream and a show, youth has gone, head shakes, the Name carries across, hold it lightly, and Rama gone. Today the ninth Guru turns to worry. Day six hundred two.
screen: `RAMA GONE — EVEN THEY WENT.`

segments.voice: A worry list, scribbled on the back of an envelope. The car is making a noise. Dad's knees are worse. The kids will leave home one day. Everyone on this list is getting older. Some of these are real problems. But read the list again and something odd shows up: much of it is not a surprise at all. It's the most predictable thing in the world. Bodies age. Things wear out. People move on. Guru Tegh Bahadur has a two-line salok about exactly this list, and it has a twist in its first line. Today: worry about the unexpected.
screen: `A WORRY LIST ON AN ENVELOPE.` → `MUCH OF IT IS NO SURPRISE.` → `A SALOK WITH A TWIST.`

segments.voice: The salok is number fifty-one among the ninth Guru's saloks near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, on Ang fourteen twenty-nine. It opens: chinta taa kee keejeeai, jo anhonee hoi. In paraphrase: worry about the thing that would be anhonee, the thing that cannot happen, the thing nobody expects. Chinta is the everyday Punjabi word for worry, the one a grandmother uses when you're late home. Anhonee is the odd one: the not-happening, the impossible. So the line sounds backwards at first. Worry only about what can't happen? Then the second line explains. Ihu maarag sansaar ko: this is the road of the world. Nanak, thir nahee koi: nothing stays, nobody stands still. Here's the turn. Change is not the anhonee. Change is what the road does every day. Aging, loss, the end of a season: these are the road itself. If something truly unexpected came along, maybe that would deserve worry. But the things we dread most are the things the world has always done. Worrying about them is like worrying that the sun will set. Notice what the Guru doesn't say. He doesn't say nothing matters, or that you shouldn't care for your father's knees. Care is one thing; chinta is another. Care takes him to the doctor. Chinta lies awake rehearsing a loss that hasn't come, as if fear could stop the road from being a road. Remember who's speaking. These saloks are traditionally linked to the last part of Guru Tegh Bahadur's life, in the time before his execution in Delhi. The calm in them isn't the calm of someone with an easy life. It's calm that looked straight at the road.
screen: `CHINTA: WORRY. ANHONEE: WHAT CAN'T HAPPEN.` · `THIS IS THE ROAD OF THE WORLD.` · `CHANGE IS NOT THE SURPRISE.` · `CARE IS ONE THING; WORRY IS ANOTHER.` · then, large: `NOTHING STAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drop one expected worry. Sit comfortably and let the list come up. Pick one worry that is really about something the world always does: getting older, a child growing up, a season ending. Name it plainly. Then ask: is there one thing I can actually do about this? If there is, note it for later. If there isn't, breathe out and set it down, the way you'd put a heavy bag on the floor. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you let it go. The bell holds the time.
Worry about the unexpected. Chinta for the anhonee: save worry for what can't happen, because change is the road itself.
screen: `WORRY ABOUT THE UNEXPECTED — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: nothing stays. The next time a predictable worry comes back today, say the line once and ask what care, not chinta, would do. Day six hundred two.

screen: `DAY 602 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHATEVER IS BORN WILL PASS.`
